## At a glance
**Guiding question:** Which target quantity answers the actual question?

**For:** clinicians and researchers who plan an analysis of routine or registry data ·
**Prerequisites:** @sec-b01 (decision map, first steps in R)

**In the course:** [W5 · Causality, trajectories and phenotypes](https://cttir.github.io/clinical-data-science-in-r-course/lessons/w5-causality-trajectories-phenotypes.html)
(required core reading); the three questions are first drafted in
[W1 · From clinical case to question](https://cttir.github.io/clinical-data-science-in-r-course/lessons/w1-from-clinical-case-to-question.html) ·
**Data:** synthetic (generated in the chapter) · **Core reading time:** about 11 minutes
:::

## Case and decision {#sec-b02-case}

A geriatric trauma team reviews its results after hip fracture surgery. The in-house standard aims to operate within
24 hours of admission (an *assumption* of this case, not a guideline statement). A colleague presents an analysis of
the intensive care database. Among older patients with hip fracture who needed intensive care, those whose surgery was
delayed beyond 24 hours were *less* often unable to walk independently at day 90. Someone suggests that the push for
early surgery could be relaxed for complex patients. The head of department has to decide whether to change the
standard. Before looking at any model, the team needs to know which question the analysis answered, and whether it is
the question the decision requires.

## Core reading {#sec-b02-core}

::: {.callout-important appearance="simple" icon=false}
**Core reading** · required for W5 · about 11 minutes · ends before ‘Lab’
:::

### Three questions about the same variables

The same variables can serve three different purposes. Hernán and colleagues call them description, prediction
and counterfactual prediction, the last being the task of causal inference [@hernan2019secondchance]. Shmueli showed
that a model built to explain is judged by different criteria from a model built to predict, even if the software
call looks the same [@shmueli2010explain]. @tbl-b02-questions applies this to the case.

| | Describe | Predict | Explain (causal) |
|:--|:--|:--|:--|
| Example | What proportion of patients aged 70 or over with hip fracture could not walk independently at day 90, by timing of surgery? | For a patient like Ms K., what is the probability at admission of not walking independently at day 90? | How would the proportion not walking at day 90 change if all patients were operated within 24 hours rather than later? |
| Time zero | Admission | Moment of prediction (here: admission) | Moment of the decision on timing (admission) |
| Target quantity | Proportions with their denominators | An individual risk; judged by accuracy and calibration | A risk difference between two hypothetical strategies |
| ‘Surgery delayed’ | Grouping variable | Predictor, if known at the moment of prediction | The intervention |
| ‘ICU admission’ | Defines a subgroup and changes the population | Not yet known at admission; a valid predictor only for a later time zero | A consequence of the intervention; must not be selected or adjusted for |

: Three questions about the same variables in the hip fracture case. The data and the software can be identical; time zero, target quantity and the role of each variable differ. {#tbl-b02-questions}

A descriptive answer is correct if the counts are right and the denominators are named. A prognostic answer is useful
if its predictions are accurate in the population where they will be used. A causal answer requires something more:
an assumption about how the variables influence each other.

### The target quantity has to be written down

For the causal question, the target quantity, the *estimand*, has to be specified before the analysis. The ICH E9(R1)
addendum lists its attributes: the treatment conditions to be compared, the population, the variable measured in each
patient, the handling of *intercurrent events* (events after the start of treatment, such as death or transfer, that
affect the measurement or its meaning) and the population-level summary [@ich2019e9r1]. For the case: older
patients admitted with hip fracture; surgery within 24 hours versus later; not walking independently at day 90; death
before day 90 counted as not walking (a composite strategy, one of several possible choices); the difference in
proportions. Hernán and Robins recommend describing the randomised trial one would ideally run, the *target trial*,
and then aligning eligibility, assignment and time zero in the observational data with it [@hernan2016targettrial].
In such a trial, nobody would be enrolled only after reaching the intensive care unit.

### A small causal diagram

@fig-b02-dag draws the assumptions as a directed acyclic graph (DAG). Each arrow means “may directly influence”; a
missing arrow is a strong claim that there is no direct influence.

```{r}
#| label: fig-b02-dag
#| echo: false
#| fig-cap: "Causal assumptions for the hip fracture case (directed acyclic graph). Each arrow is an *assumption* of this teaching example, not a finding. The role of each variable for the effect of delayed surgery on walking is given in brackets. Thick purple arrows: the path through ICU admission that opens when only ICU patients are analysed. Organ dysfunction is not recorded in the database. No sample size: the graph describes assumed structure, not data."
#| fig-alt: "Diagram with six labelled boxes. Surgery delayed more than 24 hours (exposure) on the left has arrows to not walking at day 90 (outcome) on the right, to delirium (mediator) below the middle, and to ICU admission (collider) above. Delirium points to the outcome. Frailty (confounder) at the bottom points to both the exposure and the outcome. Organ dysfunction, not measured, at the top right points to ICU admission and to the outcome."
#| fig-height: 4.2
library(ggplot2)
library(dagitty)

dag_b02 <- dagitty('dag {
  delay    [exposure, pos="0,0"]
  walk     [outcome,  pos="4,0"]
  frailty  [pos="2,1.5"]
  delirium [pos="2,0.7"]
  icu      [pos="1.5,-1.2"]
  organ    [latent, pos="3.5,-1.2"]
  frailty -> delay
  frailty -> walk
  delay -> walk
  delay -> delirium -> walk
  delay -> icu
  organ -> icu
  organ -> walk
}')

# node positions (dagitty counts y downwards, so the sign is flipped for plotting)
pos   <- coordinates(dag_b02)
nodes <- data.frame(name = names(pos$x), x = pos$x, y = -pos$y)
labels <- c(delay = "Surgery delayed > 24 h\n(exposure)", walk = "Not walking at day 90\n(outcome)",
            frailty = "Frailty\n(confounder)", delirium = "Delirium\n(mediator)",
            icu = "ICU admission\n(collider)", organ = "Organ dysfunction\n(not measured)")
nodes$label <- labels[nodes$name]

# arrows run from box edge to box edge; box half-width grows with the longest label line
longest  <- sapply(strsplit(nodes$label, "\n"), function(l) max(nchar(l)))
nodes$hw <- 0.026 * longest + 0.06          # half-width in plot units
hh <- 0.21                                  # half-height in plot units
e <- as.data.frame(edges(dag_b02))[, c("v", "w")]
from <- nodes[match(e$v, nodes$name), ]
to   <- nodes[match(e$w, nodes$name), ]
dx <- to$x - from$x; dy <- to$y - from$y; len <- sqrt(dx^2 + dy^2)
ux <- dx / len; uy <- dy / len
gap_from <- pmin(from$hw / abs(ux), hh / abs(uy)) + 0.05
gap_to   <- pmin(to$hw / abs(ux), hh / abs(uy)) + 0.05
arrows_df <- data.frame(x = from$x + gap_from * ux, y = from$y + gap_from * uy,
                        xend = to$x - gap_to * ux, yend = to$y - gap_to * uy,
                        path = ifelse(e$v == "organ" | e$w == "icu",
                                      "path through ICU admission", "other arrows"))

ggplot() +
  geom_segment(data = arrows_df,
               aes(x = x, y = y, xend = xend, yend = yend, colour = path, linewidth = path),
               arrow = arrow(length = unit(2.4, "mm"), type = "closed")) +
  geom_label(data = nodes, aes(x = x, y = y, label = label), size = 3.2, linewidth = 0.3,
             fill = c(delay = "#D6E9F5", walk = "#F8DCCB", frailty = "#FBEFCC", delirium = "#CCEDE3",
                      icu = "#F2DCE9", organ = "grey92")[nodes$name]) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c("other arrows" = "grey35",
                                 "path through ICU admission" = cdsr_colours[["purple"]]), name = NULL) +
  scale_linewidth_manual(values = c("other arrows" = 0.5, "path through ICU admission" = 1.3), name = NULL) +
  coord_cartesian(xlim = c(-0.7, 4.7), ylim = c(-1.7, 1.5)) +
  theme_void(base_size = 12) + theme(legend.position = "bottom")
```

Three roles matter. **Frailty** is a *confounder*: it makes delay more likely (frail patients often need medical
optimisation first) and independently worsens walking. Comparing delayed with early surgery without accounting for
frailty mixes the two. **Delirium** is a *mediator*: it lies on a path from delay to walking. For the total effect of
delay, one does not adjust for it, because that would remove part of the effect we want to estimate.
**ICU admission** is a *collider* on the path delay → ICU ← organ dysfunction → walking: two arrows collide in it.
That path is closed as long as we leave ICU admission alone. Selecting only ICU patients, or adjusting for ICU
admission, opens it [@hernan2004selection]. The R package **dagitty** reads such a graph and lists the variables
that are sufficient for adjustment [@textor2016dagitty]; here the answer is frailty alone.

### Why the sign flips

In the Lab we simulate 4,000 patients whose data follow exactly this graph. The true effect of delay is built in:
7.5 percentage points more patients not walking at day 90 (*assumption*). In the whole cohort, after adjusting for
frailty, the estimate is +7.2 points. Among the 767 ICU patients alone it is −9.9 points: delay seems protective
(both *synthetic*).

The explanation lies in why patients reach the ICU. Patients operated early usually got there because of organ
dysfunction; in the simulation this applies to 81% of them. Patients with delayed surgery often got there because of
complications of the waiting time, and only 40% had organ dysfunction. Organ dysfunction strongly impairs recovery.
Within the ICU, the early-surgery group is therefore sicker, and delay looks favourable. The same mechanism has been
described for studies that sampled only hospitalised or tested patients during the COVID-19 pandemic
[@griffith2020collider].

### What would answer the head of department

The ICU analysis is not useless; it correctly describes patients who reached intensive care. It cannot answer the
question on the table, because the decision about timing is taken at admission and applies to all admitted patients.
An analysis that could inform the standard starts at admission (time zero), includes every older patient admitted
with hip fracture, compares surgery within 24 hours with later surgery, adjusts for the confounders named in the
graph (here frailty), treats death before day 90 according to the estimand, and does not select or adjust on
anything that happens after the timing decision, including ICU admission and delirium. If organ dysfunction at
admission were recorded, it would be measured before the decision and could be used as well; recorded after the
decision, it would be a consequence. The whole difference lies in the order of events, which is why time zero comes
first.

**The DAG is an assumption, not a result. The data alone cannot show whether delay causes ICU admission; clinical
knowledge has to justify that arrow, and with it the decision not to analyse ICU patients separately.**

**Question for the workshop:** Which of the three questions does the head of department need answered? Write down
its time zero, its population and the one variable you would refuse to select on — and say why.

## Lab {#sec-b02-lab}

### Step 1: the graph as an R object

The DAG in @fig-b02-dag was defined with the following code (the drawing part is ordinary **ggplot2**).

```{r}
#| label: b02-dag-code
#| ref.label: fig-b02-dag
#| eval: false
```

**dagitty** can now answer questions about the graph. `adjustmentSets()` lists the minimal sets of variables that
block every non-causal path between exposure and outcome; `isAdjustmentSet()` tests a proposed set.

```{r}
#| label: b02-adjustment
adjustmentSets(dag_b02, effect = "total")
checks <- c(
  frailty              = isAdjustmentSet(dag_b02, "frailty"),
  frailty_and_icu      = isAdjustmentSet(dag_b02, c("frailty", "icu")),
  frailty_and_delirium = isAdjustmentSet(dag_b02, c("frailty", "delirium"))
)
checks
stopifnot(identical(unname(checks), c(TRUE, FALSE, FALSE)))
```

Adding ICU admission breaks the adjustment because it opens the collider path. Adding delirium breaks it for the
*total* effect because it blocks part of the effect itself. `paths()` shows which paths are open after selecting on
ICU admission:

```{r}
#| label: b02-paths
paths(dag_b02, Z = c("frailty", "icu"))
```

The path `delay -> icu <- organ -> walk` is listed as open (`TRUE`). The back-door path through frailty is closed.

### Step 2: data that follow the graph

The function below simulates patients exactly as the graph says. Every number in it is a teaching *assumption*. Each
line draws one variable with `rbinom()`, which returns 1 (yes) with the stated probability and 0 (no) otherwise. The
seed inside the function makes the result identical on every computer.

```{r}
#| label: b02-simulate
simulate_cohort <- function(n = 4000, delay_to_icu = 0.25, seed = 2402) {
  set.seed(seed)
  frailty  <- rbinom(n, 1, 0.40)                                   # 40% frail
  organ    <- rbinom(n, 1, 0.20)                                   # 20% acute organ dysfunction
  delay    <- rbinom(n, 1, 0.25 + 0.20 * frailty)                  # frailty -> delay
  delirium <- rbinom(n, 1, 0.15 + 0.15 * delay)                    # delay -> delirium
  icu      <- rbinom(n, 1, 0.03 + delay_to_icu * delay + 0.45 * organ)   # delay, organ -> ICU
  not_walk <- rbinom(n, 1, 0.10 + 0.06 * delay + 0.10 * delirium + 0.15 * frailty + 0.35 * organ)
  data.frame(frailty, organ, delay, delirium, icu, not_walk)
}
cohort <- simulate_cohort()
true_effect <- 0.06 + 0.10 * 0.15          # direct part + part through delirium
c(patients = nrow(cohort), icu = sum(cohort$icu), true_effect = true_effect)
```

The true total effect is 0.06 (direct) plus 0.10 × 0.15 (the extra delirium caused by delay, times the harm of
delirium) = 0.075, i.e. 7.5 percentage points.

### Step 3: three analyses, three answers

A linear model with a 0/1 outcome, `lm(not_walk ~ delay + frailty)`, returns the risk difference for delay directly as
its coefficient. This is enough for a simulation in which all effects add up; it is not a general recommendation for
binary outcomes ([Methods in R: Multiple Linear Regression](https://cttir.github.io/methods-in-r/sec-ch-07-regression.html#sec-chapters-07-regression-multiple-linear-regression)
explains the model).

```{r}
#| label: b02-estimates
risk_diff <- function(formula, data) coef(lm(formula, data = data))[["delay"]]
estimates <- c(
  describe_all          = risk_diff(not_walk ~ delay, cohort),
  adjust_frailty        = risk_diff(not_walk ~ delay + frailty, cohort),
  adjust_frailty_delir  = risk_diff(not_walk ~ delay + frailty + delirium, cohort),
  icu_only              = risk_diff(not_walk ~ delay + frailty, cohort[cohort$icu == 1, ])
)
round(100 * estimates, 1)   # percentage points
stopifnot(round(100 * estimates[["adjust_frailty"]], 1) == 7.2,
          round(100 * estimates[["icu_only"]], 1) == -9.9,
          sum(cohort$icu) == 767)
```

The crude difference (+`r round(100 * estimates[["describe_all"]], 1)` points) is a correct *description* of this
cohort but overstates the effect, because frail patients are delayed more often. Adjusting for frailty gives
+`r round(100 * estimates[["adjust_frailty"]], 1)` points, close to the built-in 7.5. Adding delirium gives
+`r round(100 * estimates[["adjust_frailty_delir"]], 1)` points: roughly the direct part only. Restricting to ICU
patients reverses the sign.

### Step 4: explaining the sign

```{r}
#| label: b02-sign
organ_share <- rbind(
  all_patients = tapply(cohort$organ, cohort$delay, mean),
  icu_only     = tapply(cohort$organ[cohort$icu == 1], cohort$delay[cohort$icu == 1], mean)
)
colnames(organ_share) <- c("early surgery", "delayed surgery")
round(organ_share, 2)
stopifnot(round(organ_share["icu_only", ], 2) == c(0.81, 0.40))
```

In the whole cohort, organ dysfunction is equally common with and without delay (about 20%), as the graph demands.
Among ICU patients, it is twice as common after early surgery. Because organ dysfunction adds 35 percentage points to
the risk of not walking, the early-surgery ICU patients do worse, and delay appears protective. The negative sign is
not a property of delay. It is a property of the selection.

### Step 5: is it chance?

One simulated cohort could be unlucky. Repeating the simulation with 100 different seeds shows how stable the sign
is.

```{r}
#| label: b02-repeat
icu_estimates <- sapply(1:100, function(s) {
  d <- simulate_cohort(seed = s)
  risk_diff(not_walk ~ delay + frailty, d[d$icu == 1, ])
})
share_negative <- mean(icu_estimates < 0)
round(c(median = median(icu_estimates), share_negative = share_negative), 3)
stopifnot(share_negative >= 0.90)
```

In `r round(100 * share_negative)` of 100 repetitions the ICU-only estimate is negative, although delay harms every
simulated patient group. Selection, not chance, drives the result.

### Step 6: the prognostic question uses the same data differently

For prediction, the question is not whether a coefficient is causal but whether predicted risks are accurate for new
patients. A logistic model with the two variables that the database records at admission, frailty and timing of
surgery, gives a risk for a patient like Ms K.: frail and operated early.

```{r}
#| label: b02-predict
fit_prog <- glm(not_walk ~ frailty + delay, family = binomial, data = cohort)
ms_k <- data.frame(frailty = 1, delay = 0)
risk_ms_k <- predict(fit_prog, newdata = ms_k, type = "response")
round(risk_ms_k, 3)
built_in <- 0.10 + 0.15 + 0.10 * 0.15 + 0.35 * 0.20   # baseline + frailty + delirium + average organ part
stopifnot(abs(risk_ms_k - built_in) < 0.03)
```

The predicted risk of about `r cdsr_percent(risk_ms_k)` is close to the average risk built into the simulation for
such patients (`r cdsr_percent(built_in)`). The model does not know about organ dysfunction, yet it can still be a
reasonable *average* prediction. Whether it is good enough for a decision is a question of calibration and clinical
utility (@sec-b06), not of causal structure.

::: {.callout-warning title="Common mistake"}
Reporting every coefficient of one adjusted model as if each were a causal effect (sometimes called the “Table 2
fallacy”). In Step 3, the model `not_walk ~ delay + frailty` is built for the effect of delay. Its frailty coefficient
does not estimate the effect of frailty, because part of that effect runs through delay. Each causal question needs
its own adjustment set ([Methods in R: DAGs](https://cttir.github.io/methods-in-r/sec-appendices-e-cheatsheets.html#sec-appendices-e-cheatsheets-dags)).
:::

## Counter-check {#sec-b02-countercheck}

Change one assumption: delay no longer causes ICU admission (`delay_to_icu = 0`), for example because the ward now
has a dedicated orthogeriatric team that manages complications without intensive care. ICU admission then depends
only on organ dysfunction. **Predict first:** what happens to the ICU-only estimate — does it stay negative, move
towards +7.5, or overshoot?

```{r}
#| label: b02-countercheck
cohort_no_arrow <- simulate_cohort(delay_to_icu = 0)
counter <- c(
  icu_only_with_arrow    = estimates[["icu_only"]],
  icu_only_without_arrow = risk_diff(not_walk ~ delay + frailty, cohort_no_arrow[cohort_no_arrow$icu == 1, ])
)
round(100 * counter, 1)
stopifnot(counter[["icu_only_without_arrow"]] > 0)
```

Without the arrow from delay to ICU, ICU admission is no longer a collider between delay and organ dysfunction, and
the ICU-only estimate is positive again (`r round(100 * counter[["icu_only_without_arrow"]], 1)` points, with more
random noise because only about 760 patients remain). The data could not have told us which of the two worlds we are
in; only the clinical argument about the arrow can.

## Consequences for patients and operations {#sec-b02-consequences}

**Patients.** Read causally, the ICU analysis would suggest that delaying surgery is harmless or even beneficial for
complex patients. In the simulated world the opposite is true, and frail patients would bear the harm of a relaxed
standard. An analysis restricted by its data source (here: the ICU database) has selected its population before any
model was fitted. That restriction must be reported as prominently as the result.

**Operations.** A department that changes a standard on the basis of routine data should ask for three things before
the meeting: the written estimand, the DAG with a justification for each arrow, and the inclusion criteria of the
data source. Prediction models may use post-admission information if their time zero is later; such a model should
state its time zero in its name and documentation.

**Ethics and regulation.** Presenting a prognostic association as a treatment recommendation is an error with
ethical weight, because it shifts risk to patients without evidence. If a prognostic model were used to steer
individual treatment decisions, its intended purpose could make it a medical device under the MDR
[@eu2017mdr]; this is examined in @sec-b22. Data protection is touched only indirectly; secondary use of routine data
for such analyses is the subject of @sec-b23 and @sec-b26.

## Look up and transfer {#sec-b02-lookup}

- **Reviewer question:** Which variables were conditioned on by the design or the data source (inclusion criteria,
  registry, database) rather than in the model — and could any of them be a consequence of the exposure?
- **Self-test:** A geriatric rehabilitation clinic analyses its own patients after hip fracture. Patients with
  dementia regain walking faster than patients without dementia. The clinic admits patients only if they had good
  mobility before the fracture *or* good cognitive function. Why might dementia look favourable, and what is the
  collider?

  ::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Answer"}
  Admission to the clinic is a collider: both pre-fracture mobility and cognitive function lead to admission. Among
  admitted patients, those with dementia must have had very good pre-fracture mobility, otherwise they would not have
  been admitted. Good pre-fracture mobility predicts faster recovery, so dementia appears favourable. The sign is
  produced by the admission rule, not by dementia. A population-based cohort starting at the fracture (time zero)
  avoids this selection.
  :::
